sbh3.2:4.4: meaning, substance, characteristic, side, time, and reasoning. Having sought these, he reviews them.
sbh3.2:5.2: 'The meaning of this teaching is this; the meaning of this teaching is that' — thus he seeks meaning.
sbh3.2:5.12: Side is twofold: dark side and bright side.
sbh3.2:5.13: The dark side is investigated as fault,

sbh3.2:5.26: dependence-reasoning, cause-and-effect reasoning, proof-establishing reasoning, and nature-of-things reasoning.
sbh3.2:5.27: By dependence-reasoning he investigates the conventional as conventional,
sbh3.2:5.31: By cause-and-effect reasoning he investigates the function of phenomena:
sbh3.2:5.32: 'This is the dharma; this is its function; this is its function.'
sbh3.2:5.33: By proof-establishing reasoning he investigates by means of the three *pramāṇas* (valid means of knowing):
sbh3.2:5.34: trustworthy testimony, inference, and direct perception.
sbh3.2:5.36: Is there a self here, or not? Is it apprehended by direct perception, or not? Is it established by inference, or not?'

sbh3.2:6.1: This is the *vipaśyanā* with the six investigation-subjects and three gateways, in summary.
sbh3.2:6.5: Three kinds of comprehension are intended: comprehension of the meaning of what is taught; comprehension of 'as far as it goes' of the substance;
sbh3.2:6.6: and comprehension of 'as it actually is.'
sbh3.2:6.7: The investigation of meaning yields comprehension of what is taught.
sbh3.2:6.8: The investigation of substance and the investigation of specific characteristic together yield comprehension of how far the substance extends.
sbh3.2:6.9: The investigation of general characteristic, of side, of time and reasoning together yield comprehension of how things actually are.
sbh3.2:6.10: This much is to be known by the practitioner:
sbh3.2:6.11: namely, the meaning of what is taught; and the *yāvad-bhāvikatā* of the substance to be known,
sbh3.2:7.1: The practitioner engaged in foulness investigates the six investigation-subjects.
sbh3.2:7.3: Taking what he has heard and grasped about foulness as governing, with attention concentrated on its plane, he comprehends the meaning thus:
sbh3.2:7.4: 'This foulness — this is repulsive, this is disgusting, this is foul-smelling, this is putrid.'
sbh3.2:7.5: By such aspects [there is] comprehension of the meaning of the foulness-teaching previously heard.
sbh3.2:7.6: Thus he investigates the meaning by way of foulness.
sbh3.2:8.1: How does he investigate the substance?
sbh3.2:8.2: Comprehending the meaning, he sees this foulness as established in two locations: inwardly and outwardly.
sbh3.2:9.1: How does he investigate the specific characteristic?
sbh3.2:9.2: Inwardly, he resolves on the foulness-as-such of the foulness within the body:
sbh3.2:9.3: 'There exist in this body: hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, dust, dirt, skin, flesh, bone, sinew, vein, kidneys, heart, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach contents, bowel contents, urine, feces, tears, sweat, saliva, mucus, fat, lymph, marrow, grease, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, brain, cranial fluid, urine.'
sbh3.2:9.4: He further resolves that this multifold inward-body foulness is comprised by two elements:
sbh3.2:9.5: the earth element and the water element.
sbh3.2:9.7: through liver and feces — this he resolves as the earth element.
sbh3.2:9.8: From tears and lymph through urine — this he resolves as the water element.
sbh3.2:10.1: Outwardly, he resolves on the foulness as found outside the body, by way of aspects beginning with the discolored.
sbh3.2:10.3: a corpse he has himself seen,
sbh3.2:10.4: or heard described, or imagined — of a woman, a man, a friend, an enemy, or one indifferent to him;
sbh3.2:10.5: low, middling, or excellent; young, middle-aged, or elderly.
sbh3.2:10.6: Taking the sign, he resolves on a corpse one day dead, blood having clotted, just turning to pus — as the discolored.
sbh3.2:10.7: A corpse two days dead, fully turned to pus, before worms have arisen — as the festering.
sbh3.2:10.8: A corpse seven days dead, with worms arisen, swollen, fully bloated — as the swollen.
sbh3.2:10.9: A corpse being eaten by crows, vultures, dogs, jackals — as the gnawed.
sbh3.2:10.10: A corpse with skin, flesh, and blood gone, only sinews holding the bones together — as the bloody-skeletal.
sbh3.2:10.11: When the limbs have been scattered in different directions and pulled apart — bones with flesh, bones without flesh, bones with little flesh remaining — as the dispersed.
sbh3.2:11.1: Furthermore, there are two skeletons: the body-skeleton and the limb-skeleton.
sbh3.2:11.2: The body-skeleton runs from the pelvis up the spine to where the skull rests.
sbh3.2:11.3: The limb-skeleton is the connected arm-bones and thigh-and-leg bones.
sbh3.2:11.4: The body-skeleton is properly called the *śaṅkalikā*;
sbh3.2:11.6: Furthermore, two skeleton-signs may be taken: the painted, the stone-and-wood-carved,
sbh3.2:11.10: [when he attends to the not-actually-existing,] he resolves only on the *śaṅkalikā*, not on the *asthi-śaṅkalikā*.
sbh3.2:11.11: When he attends to the sign of the actually-existing skeleton,
sbh3.2:12.1: This outward color-form has three kinds of change:
sbh3.2:12.3: change-by-another, and change of both kinds.
sbh3.2:12.4: From the discolored through the swollen — that is change-by-its-own-nature.
sbh3.2:12.5: From the gnawed through the dispersed — that is change-by-another.
sbh3.2:12.6: The bones and the skeleton — that is change of both kinds.
sbh3.2:12.7: One who thus knows directly the outward foulness in this aspect investigates the specific characteristic of outward foulness in just this aspect.
sbh3.2:13.1: How does he investigate the general characteristic of foulness?
sbh3.2:13.2: Just as inwardly the body's color-form is unaltered foul-color [in some respects] and outwardly the body's color-form is altered foul-color [in others], he resolves that they share the same nature and the same property:
sbh3.2:13.3: 'This unaltered color-form is also of this nature.'
sbh3.2:13.4: Whatever beings possess this fair color-form — they too have it of just this nature, of the kind belonging to outward foulness.
sbh3.2:14.1: How does he investigate the side?
sbh3.2:14.3: 'If I, [in regard to] this fair color-form, [generate] this foul-nature,'
sbh3.2:14.4: 'not knowing it as it is — neither as inward nor as outward foul color-form — should generate craving for fair color-form, that is mere perversion, gathered into the dark side.'
sbh3.2:14.5: 'It produces escape-by-suffering, with affliction, with calamity, with burning.'
sbh3.2:14.6: 'From this arise, in time to come, birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.'
sbh3.2:14.7: 'Whereas the seeing-as-it-is of the foulness-nature within fair color-form is the bright side.'
sbh3.2:14.8: 'This dharma is without suffering, without affliction; from this, despair through to all subsequent suffering ceases.'
sbh3.2:14.9: 'Therefore, what is the dark-side condition is not to be tolerated; it is to be abandoned, purified.'
sbh3.2:14.10: 'The bright-side, when not arisen, is to be aroused;'
sbh3.2:14.11: 'when arisen, its abiding, growth, abundance, and amplitude are to be made.'
sbh3.2:15.3: 'This inward fair color-form is so taking the present time. This outward foul color-form is also so taking the present time.'
sbh3.2:15.5: '[the outward foul one] was a fair color-form.'
sbh3.2:15.6: 'As that was — taking past time — fair, just as I am now',
sbh3.2:15.8: 'so by progression, taking present time, [the present fair one] has become foul. This fair color-form of mine, taking present time, is foul.'
sbh3.2:15.9: 'It will not, in time-to-come, not be foul —'
sbh3.2:15.11: 'As is this outward [body], so is mine taking present time.'
sbh3.2:15.12: Thus through past, future, and present times: 'this body of mine is of such a nature, has been such, will be such, and does not transcend this nature.' Thus he investigates time.
sbh3.2:16.3: 'There is no self, no being, inward or outward, that could be either fair or foul.'
sbh3.2:16.4: 'Rather, this is mere form — mere accumulation of itching and scratching — wherein this notion, this designation, this convention is applied':
sbh3.2:16.8: 'then it lies cast off like an unconscious log.'
sbh3.2:16.9: 'Of this dead one, by stages, these altered states are to be known:'
sbh3.2:16.10: 'the discolored through the bone-skeleton stages. This body of mine —'
sbh3.2:16.12: 'born of mother-and-father impurities, accumulated by gruel and barley —'
sbh3.2:16.13: 'by what cause, by what condition, is this present-time fair color-form known as fair?'
sbh3.2:16.14: 'But the inward body is at all times, both inwardly and outwardly, foul.' Thus by way of the conventional, the ultimate, and the causal,
sbh3.2:17.1: It occurs to him: 'This foulness, thus practiced, cultivated, made much of, conduces to the abandonment of sensual craving.'
sbh3.2:17.2: 'And sensual craving is to be abandoned.'
sbh3.2:17.3: Thus he investigates by cause-and-effect reasoning.
sbh3.2:17.4: It occurs to him: 'It has been spoken by the Blessed One:
sbh3.2:17.5: Foulness practiced, cultivated, made much of, conduces to the abandonment of sensual craving. This, for me, is the trustworthy testimony.'
sbh3.2:17.7: 'as I, however much, cultivate foulness and attend to it,'
sbh3.2:17.8: 'thus the obsession of sensual craving — when not arisen — does not arise;'
sbh3.2:17.11: 'when one attends to a counter-aspect dharma,'
sbh3.2:17.12: 'defilement arises through the object of the counter-aspect.'
sbh3.2:17.13: Thus he investigates by proof-establishing reasoning.
sbh3.2:17.15: 'This is an established nature-of-things, an unthinkable nature-of-things:'
sbh3.2:17.16: 'that foulness-cultivation is the antidote to the abandonment of sensual craving.'
sbh3.2:17.20: Thus by nature-of-things reasoning he investigates foulness.
sbh3.2:17.21: This is the threefold-gateway, six-investigation-subject *vipaśyanā* of one engaged in foulness.
sbh3.2:18.1: How does the practitioner engaged in lovingkindness investigate the six investigation-subjects?
sbh3.2:18.2: Taking the lovingkindness-teaching as governing, comprehending the meaning of 'lovingkindness — characterized by the resolve to bring happiness to all, established in benefit-and-happiness-aspiration' — he investigates the meaning.
sbh3.2:19.1: He, comprehending the meaning, investigates closely: 'This is the friend-side; this is the enemy-side; this is the indifferent-side.'
sbh3.2:19.2: 'All these sides, falling within the continuum of others, are outward substance' — so he resolves.
sbh3.2:19.3: Or: friend-side as inward, enemy-and-indifferent-side as outward. Thus he investigates lovingkindness in the substance.
sbh3.2:20.2: 'These three sides — neither suffering nor happy,'
sbh3.2:20.4: Among these: the friend is characterized by helpfulness;
sbh3.2:20.7: Among those who are not-suffering-and-happy and who desire happiness, three kinds of happiness-desire are known:
sbh3.2:20.8: some desire sensual happiness; some desire form-realm happiness with rapture; some desire form-realm happiness without rapture.
sbh3.2:20.9: Of those who are afflicted by sensual happiness:
sbh3.2:20.11: Likewise of those wishing rapture-happiness or rapture-less happiness.
sbh3.2:20.12: Thus by way of specific characteristic he investigates lovingkindness.
sbh3.2:21.3: 'equanimity-of-mind is to be made by me,'
sbh3.2:21.6: 'With the friend, bringing happiness is not difficult for me —'
sbh3.2:21.9: 'with that also, not very difficult for me.'
sbh3.2:21.12: 'So bringing happiness is to be made by me here above all.'
sbh3.2:21.16: 'In this case, no one actually scolds or is scolded,'
sbh3.2:21.20: 'apart from these letters of speech that resound.'
sbh3.2:21.21: 'They are mere syllables, mere measure-of-syllable. And this body, of form, gross, made of the four great elements — it is here that such contacts come to me, [I] standing here:'
sbh3.2:21.23: 'contacts of hand, clod, stick, weapon. This body of mine —'
sbh3.2:21.24: 'is impermanent; these contacts that harm — these too are impermanent.'
sbh3.2:21.26: 'all beings are subject to birth, aging, illness, death; by their very nature they suffer. It would be unbecoming for me,'
sbh3.2:21.27: 'if to beings already naturally suffering, I should bring further suffering rather than happiness — that would be like an enemy acting on a friend, since these beings already do this to themselves.'
sbh3.2:22.1: Furthermore, it has been spoken by the Blessed One:
sbh3.2:22.2: 'I do not see any easily-found being'
sbh3.2:22.3: 'who, in this long course of *saṁsāra*, has not been my mother, father, brother, sister, teacher, preceptor, or one in the position of a guru.'
sbh3.2:22.4: Thus by this consideration also: the enemy-side is enemy-side only as a designation.
sbh3.2:22.5: There is no fixed essence here — friend-or-enemy-being. The friend, by the passage of time, becomes the enemy;
sbh3.2:22.6: the enemy too becomes the friend.
sbh3.2:22.8: the view of equality, is to be made;
sbh3.2:22.11: Thus by way of general characteristic he investigates lovingkindness.
sbh3.2:23.2: 'Whatever ill-will arises in me toward harm-doing beings — that is the death-nature' — extended at length as before.
sbh3.2:23.3: 'And whatever non-ill-will is now present — that is the deathless-nature' — extended at length as before.
sbh3.2:23.4: Thus he investigates the dark-and-bright sides of lovingkindness.
sbh3.2:24.2: 'Those happiness-desiring beings, taking past time — they have passed away. To whom shall we now bring happiness?'
sbh3.2:24.3: 'But those beings of present time — taking present time,'
sbh3.2:24.4: 'taking future time — let them be at all times happy.' Thus he investigates the time of lovingkindness.
sbh3.2:25.2: 'There is no self, no being, who would be the desirer-of-happiness,'
sbh3.2:25.3: 'or to whom happiness would be brought.'
sbh3.2:25.4: 'Rather, this is mere aggregate, mere accumulation of formations, wherein this notion, designation, convention is applied.'
sbh3.2:25.5: 'And these formations are caused by *karma* and *kleśa*.' Thus by dependence-reasoning he investigates lovingkindness.
sbh3.2:25.6: 'It is an established nature-of-things, an unthinkable nature-of-things, that lovingkindness-cultivation conduces to the abandonment of ill-will.' Thus by nature-of-things reasoning he investigates lovingkindness.
